interviewQuestions.question: What does 'superscalar' mean, and why don't processors just keep going wider (8-wide, 16-wide)?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
⭐ **Q: What does 'superscalar' mean, and why don't processors keep going wider?**

Superscalar means fetching, decoding, and issuing more than one instruction per cycle by duplicating front-end and execution hardware, vs. a scalar pipeline's one-per-cycle ceiling.

Wider stops paying off for two reasons: **available ILP** — programs don't offer N ready, independent instructions every cycle — and **structural cost** — ports, duplicated units, issue logic grow faster than linearly with width.

That's why cores plateaued around 4–8-wide, pushing on deeper ROBs and prediction instead.

**Testing:** width as a ceiling bounded by both ILP and cost.

interviewQuestions.question: What hardware changes when you go from a scalar to a superscalar pipeline?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
**Q: What hardware changes when you go from a scalar to a superscalar pipeline?**

Front end and execute get duplicated: fetch pulls multiple instruction words per cycle, decode has parallel decoders, and execute has multiple functional units — often more than one ALU plus separate load/store and branch units — so independent instructions execute the same cycle, not just fetched together.

The easy-to-overlook part is **issue logic**: deciding every cycle which candidates can legally issue together given dependences — that scheduling problem gets harder combinatorially as width grows.

**Testing:** naming concrete duplicated hardware and recognizing issue scheduling as a real cost.
